page: Google Cloud Platform g2-standard-4 is a graphics-optimized virtual machine featuring 1 NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of VRAM based on the Ada Lovelace architecture. The host compute instance is powered by an Intel Xeon CPU operating at 2.2 GHz, configured with 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores with 2.0 threads per core. System memory totals 16.0 GB of RAM, offering 4.0 GB per vCPU. Local storage is not included.

Performance profiles demonstrate a clear distinction between host CPU operations and GPU-accelerated tasks. Standard CPU benchmarks show lower-tier performance, with stress-ng single-core scoring 1197.99 and PassMark CPU reaching 3754.01. Uncached memory read bandwidth measures 26.07 GB/sec. Conversely, GPU acceleration yields top-tier metrics for machine learning tasks. Prompt processing for medium 7B model LLM inference achieves 2296.42 tokens per second, while text generation reaches 52.18 tokens per second.

The hardware combination offers a cost-efficient entry point for GPU-bound workloads that do not require heavy host CPU or memory resources. Allocating minimal host vCPUs and RAM around the NVIDIA L4 accelerator reduces resource overhead while maintaining high throughput for inference tasks. Optimal workloads include small-to-medium large language model inference, AI video processing, graphics rendering, and machine learning model deployment.
description: Google Cloud Platform g2-standard-4 is a graphics-optimized instance equipped with 1 NVIDIA L4 GPU containing 24 GB of VRAM, paired with 4 vCPUs and 16.0 GB of RAM. Powered by an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor running at 2.2 GHz across 2 physical cores, the host system provides basic compute support, while local storage is omitted. Performance data indicates modest host CPU capabilities, reflected in a PassMark CPU score of 3754.01 and a multi-core Geekbench score of 2294.0. However, GPU performance is strong for accelerated AI tasks, delivering 2296.42 tokens per second for 7B model prompt processing and 52.18 tokens per second for text generation. This balance minimizes host resource overhead, providing an efficient architecture for GPU-accelerated workloads such as medium-scale LLM inference, AI video encoding, and computer vision tasks.
